Name: taiwan_conflict_aware_lora_merging
Title: Interference Is Anisotropic: Sign-Conflict-Aware Merging of Subject LoRA Adapters for the Taiwanese Secondary Curriculum
Short Hypothesis: When four subject-specific LoRA adapters (國文 / 數學 / 自然 / 臺灣史地社會) trained on a Gemma base model are merged, degradation is NOT uniform across subjects: the culturally-grounded Taiwan-studies adapter loses the most accuracy because its delta weights both move furthest from the pretraining prior and collide most often in sign with the Chinese-literature adapter, while the Math adapter is nearly unaffected. We predict per-domain accuracy retention under TIES-Merging is rank-correlated (Spearman rho < -0.7) with the measured pairwise sign-conflict rate, and that reallocating merge coefficients in inverse proportion to measured conflict recovers a substantial fraction of the lost Taiwan-studies accuracy without harming Math.
Related Work: TIES-Merging (Yadav et al., 2023) attributes merging failure to sign disagreement between task vectors and resolves it with trim-elect-average; DARE (Yu et al., 2024) shows delta weights are highly redundant and can be randomly dropped and rescaled. Task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023) established the additive-delta view. All three are validated overwhelmingly on English, symbolic, or Western-centric benchmarks (GLUE, MMLU, code, math), and all three apply a single uniform coefficient to every expert. What is untested is whether interference is evenly distributed across experts at all. We contribute the opposite claim: interference is anisotropic and predictable from a cheap, training-free diagnostic, and the experts that suffer are exactly the ones encoding locally-specific knowledge that is under-represented and often contradicted in pretraining corpora. This is not a new merging operator dressed up in a new benchmark -- the diagnostic (per-pair sign-conflict rate, computed before any evaluation) is the object of study, and the coefficient rule is derived from it rather than tuned.
Abstract: Model merging fuses independently fine-tuned experts into one deployable model at negligible cost, and the dominant methods -- task arithmetic, TIES-Merging, DARE -- all weight every expert equally. We ask whether that uniformity is justified when the experts differ sharply in how far they must pull the base model away from its pretraining prior. Our testbed is a single school-assistant model for Taipei junior and senior high schools: four LoRA adapters over a Gemma base, covering Chinese language and literature, mathematics, natural science, and Taiwan history/geography/civics, evaluated on TMMLU+, a benchmark of real Traditional-Chinese Taiwanese examination questions. Taiwan-studies content is a uniquely sharp probe because it is sparse in pretraining data and frequently contradicted by mainland-Chinese-dominant web text, so its adapter must move the most weight; it also shares a token subspace with the Chinese-literature adapter, so its deltas are the most likely to collide. We measure per-domain accuracy retention under three merging operators and, independently, the layer-wise pairwise sign-conflict rate between every adapter pair. We test whether conflict predicts retention, and whether a coefficient rule derived from the measured conflict matrix -- rather than tuned on the test set -- recovers Taiwan-studies accuracy without degrading mathematics. If interference is anisotropic and predictable, uniform merging is the wrong default for every localized deployment, and the fix costs one cheap diagnostic pass.

Experiments.Description: Setup and baseline. Load BASE_MODEL in bf16 with device_map={'': 0} (never fp32, never device_map='auto' -- the GPUs are shared with local inference servers and fp32 loading has OOM-killed every prior attempt). Build four domains from real TMMLU+ (`ikala/tmmluplus`) test splits: chinese = junior_chinese_exam + chinese_language_and_literature + tve_chinese_language; math = junior_math_exam + tve_mathematics; taiwan = geography_of_taiwan + junior_social_studies + jce_humanities; science = junior_science_exam + junior_chemistry + secondary_physics. Split each domain 60/40 into train/held-out. Score four-way multiple choice by comparing the logits of the A/B/C/D tokens at the final position -- one forward pass, no free-form generation, no LLM judge.
Experiments.Metrics: Zero-shot base-model accuracy per domain, reported against the 0.25 random-choice floor. Row counts per domain must be printed and non-zero.

Experiments.Description: Train one LoRA adapter per domain (rank 8, alpha 16, target q/k/v/o_proj, 2 epochs, AdamW, plain torch loop -- do NOT use Trainer, trl, or bitsandbytes; trl and bitsandbytes are not installed and transformers 5.x renamed evaluation_strategy to eval_strategy). After each adapter, extract its LoRA A/B factors to CPU and call unload() so the base model is byte-identical before the next adapter.
Experiments.Metrics: Per-epoch training loss and held-out validation loss per domain (printed as 'Epoch {n}: validation_loss = {x}'), and single-adapter accuracy on its own domain. Each adapter must beat the base model on its own domain, otherwise the merging question is moot.

Experiments.Description: Cross-domain interference matrix. Apply each adapter alone and evaluate it on ALL four held-out sets. This separates 'the adapter helps its own subject' from 'the adapter damages other subjects', and gives the per-adapter reference accuracy that retention is measured against.
Experiments.Metrics: 4x4 accuracy matrix (adapter applied x domain evaluated). Off-diagonal drop relative to base per pair.

Experiments.Description: Merge all four adapters with three operators at equal coefficients: task arithmetic (plain sum), TIES-Merging (trim to top-20% by magnitude, elect sign by summed signed magnitude, average only sign-agreeing entries), and DARE-TIES (drop each delta entry with p=0.5 and rescale by 1/(1-p), then TIES). Evaluate every merged model on all four held-out sets.
Experiments.Metrics: Per-domain accuracy and per-domain retention = merged_accuracy / single_adapter_accuracy. Mean retention across domains per operator. Headline claim requires retention on `taiwan` to be visibly lower than on `math` under at least two of the three operators.

Experiments.Description: The diagnostic. For every adapter pair and every LoRA-targeted module, compute the sign-conflict rate: among coordinates surviving the top-20% magnitude trim in BOTH deltas, the fraction whose signs disagree. Average over modules to get a 4x4 conflict matrix. This is computed from weights alone, before any evaluation, and costs no forward passes.
Experiments.Metrics: 4x4 sign-conflict matrix. Spearman rank correlation between a domain's mean conflict against the other three and its TIES retention; the hypothesis predicts rho < -0.7.

Experiments.Description: Conflict-aware coefficients. Set each domain's merge coefficient inversely proportional to its mean measured conflict against the others (normalized to sum to 1), re-merge with TIES, and re-evaluate. Coefficients are derived from the conflict matrix only -- never tuned on held-out accuracy. Compare against equal coefficients and against a control that permutes the coefficients across domains, which isolates 'conflict carries signal' from 'non-uniform coefficients happen to help'.
Experiments.Metrics: Change in `taiwan` retention and in `math` retention versus equal coefficients, and versus the permuted-coefficient control. Success = taiwan retention improves by >= 3 accuracy points while math retention drops by <= 1 point, and the permuted control does not reproduce the gain.

Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect may be small at the 1B scale used for the search loop. Mitigation: the diagnostic (sign-conflict matrix) is scale-independent and is reported even if the accuracy gap is not significant; the confirmation run repeats at 27B.

TMMLU+ multiple-choice accuracy near the 0.25 floor would make retention ratios unstable. Mitigation: report absolute accuracies alongside ratios and refuse to report retention for any domain where the single-adapter accuracy is below 0.30.

Training on multiple-choice answer letters teaches format as much as subject knowledge, so gains may partly reflect answer-format adaptation. Mitigation: the base-model baseline uses the identical prompt format, so format adaptation is shared by all conditions and cancels in the retention ratio.
The `taiwan` domain draws on geography and civics as well as history; TMMLU+ has no pure Taiwan-history subset. This is a limitation of the benchmark and is stated rather than worked around.

Sign-conflict is one of several plausible interference mechanisms; delta magnitude is a confound. Mitigation: report per-domain delta Frobenius norm alongside conflict and check whether conflict predicts retention after controlling for norm.

Name: curriculum_level_hierarchical_merging
Title: Merge Within Grade Level First: Hierarchical LoRA Fusion for Junior- and Senior-High Taiwanese Curriculum
Short Hypothesis: Adapters for the same subject at different grade levels (國中 vs 高中) are far more compatible than adapters for different subjects at the same level, so a two-stage merge -- fuse within grade level first, then fuse the two level-models -- retains more accuracy than merging all adapters in one flat step, at identical parameter cost.
Related Work: Flat merging treats all task vectors as exchangeable members of one pool. Hierarchical and grouped merging has been explored for model soups and for mixture-of-experts routing, but grouping is normally chosen by architecture or by clustering on delta similarity rather than by an externally-given structure. Curriculum data comes with a structure that is free, principled, and known in advance: grade level. TMMLU+ separates junior-high (`junior_*`) from senior-high and vocational (`tve_*`, `chinese_language_and_literature`, `secondary_physics`) subsets, so the grouping is given by the benchmark rather than inferred, which removes the usual circularity in evaluating grouped merging.
Abstract: Merging methods pool all task vectors into a single flat average, implicitly assuming every pair of experts interferes to the same degree. Educational content violates this assumption in a structured, externally-verifiable way: the same subject at two grade levels shares vocabulary, notation, and reasoning style, whereas two subjects at the same level may share almost nothing. We test whether respecting that structure improves merging. Using TMMLU+, we build six LoRA adapters over a Gemma base -- Chinese, Mathematics, and Social/Taiwan studies, each at junior-high and senior-high level -- and compare flat merging of all six against a two-stage hierarchical merge that fuses within grade level first and then fuses the two resulting level-models. We measure per-adapter and per-level accuracy retention, and we test the mechanism directly by comparing within-subject-across-level delta cosine similarity against within-level-across-subject similarity. Because the grouping is dictated by the benchmark's own subset labels rather than inferred from the deltas, a positive result cannot be explained by having fit the grouping to the evaluation. The practical payoff is a deployable model for a school that spans both grade levels, and the scientific payoff is evidence on whether known task taxonomy beats delta-space clustering as a grouping signal for merging.

Experiments.Description: Build six domains from TMMLU+ crossing three subjects with two grade levels: chinese_junior = junior_chinese_exam; chinese_senior = chinese_language_and_literature + tve_chinese_language; math_junior = junior_math_exam; math_senior = tve_mathematics; social_junior = junior_social_studies; social_senior = geography_of_taiwan + jce_humanities. Split 60/40 train/held-out. Same bf16, device_map={'': 0}, logit-comparison MCQ scoring, one-hour budget as in the primary idea.
Experiments.Metrics: Per-domain row counts and base-model zero-shot accuracy. Any domain with fewer than 80 held-out rows must be flagged.

Experiments.Description: Train six LoRA adapters (rank 8, alpha 16, q/k/v/o_proj, 2 epochs, plain torch loop). Extract A/B factors and unload after each.
Experiments.Metrics: Per-epoch validation loss per domain and single-adapter accuracy on its own held-out set.

Experiments.Description: Measure the structure before using it. Compute pairwise cosine similarity between flattened deltas for all 15 adapter pairs, and group them into within-subject-across-level pairs versus within-level-across-subject pairs.
Experiments.Metrics: Mean cosine similarity for each group, with the gap between them. The hypothesis requires within-subject-across-level similarity to exceed within-level-across-subject similarity.

Experiments.Description: Flat baseline: TIES-merge all six adapters in one step with equal coefficients. Hierarchical: TIES-merge the three junior adapters into one junior model and the three senior adapters into one senior model, then TIES-merge those two. A third arm merges within subject first (chinese_junior + chinese_senior, etc.) and then across subjects, which is the alternative grouping and the fairest control.
Experiments.Metrics: Per-domain accuracy and retention (merged / single-adapter) for all three arms, and mean retention. Success = hierarchical grouping beats flat by >= 2 mean accuracy points, and the two grouping orders are compared rather than only the favourable one being reported.

Experiments.Description: Control for merge-count confound. Hierarchical merging averages fewer vectors per step than flat merging, which alone could change the outcome. Re-run the flat baseline restricted to random three-adapter subsets and to a random two-stage grouping with the same branching factor as the hierarchical arm.
Experiments.Metrics: Mean retention of the random-grouping control versus the curriculum-grouping arm. The curriculum grouping must beat random grouping, not merely beat flat merging.

Risk Factors and Limitations: TMMLU+ junior subsets are small (126-213 held-out rows each), so per-domain accuracy has wide error bars. Mitigation: report accuracy with binomial confidence intervals and run three seeds.
The junior/senior split in TMMLU+ is imperfect -- tve_* subsets are vocational rather than strictly senior-high. This is stated as a labelling limitation rather than silently ignored.

If within-subject and within-level similarities turn out to be indistinguishable, the hierarchical arm has no mechanism to exploit and the result will be null. That null is still reported, since it is evidence against curriculum taxonomy as a grouping signal.

Six adapters instead of four roughly doubles training time; at the 1B search scale this stays inside the one-hour node budget, but the 27B confirmation run must reduce to four adapters or raise the timeout.

Name: taiwan_merge_operator_benchmark
Title: A Reproducible Baseline: Merge-Operator and Density Sweep for Taiwanese Curriculum LoRA Adapters on TMMLU+
Short Hypothesis: Across merge operators (task arithmetic, TIES, DARE-TIES) and sparsity settings (trim density, DARE drop probability), the operator ranking established on English benchmarks does not transfer unchanged to Traditional-Chinese Taiwanese curriculum content, and the optimal trim density is lower than the commonly-cited 20% because the culturally-specific deltas are less redundant.
Related Work: TIES and DARE both report that delta weights are extremely redundant -- DARE drops 90-99% of entries with no loss on English benchmarks -- and downstream practitioners adopt those hyperparameters as defaults. Redundancy, however, is a property of how much of the delta is re-encoding something the base model already knows. For content that is sparse or contradicted in pretraining, the delta should carry more irreducible information and tolerate less pruning. No published sweep exists for Traditional-Chinese localized curriculum content. This idea deliberately contributes a careful, reproducible baseline rather than a new operator; it is the safety net that makes the other two ideas interpretable, and it is scoped so that a null result is still publishable as a transfer study.
Abstract: Merging hyperparameters -- which operator, how aggressively to sparsify -- are usually inherited as defaults from papers validated on English benchmarks. We test whether those defaults transfer to a localized setting. We train four subject LoRA adapters over a Gemma base for the Taiwanese junior/senior high curriculum and evaluate the full cross product of three merge operators and a sweep over trim density and DARE drop probability, measured on TMMLU+ examination questions. Alongside accuracy we report the redundancy of each domain's delta directly, as the fraction of its Frobenius norm retained after top-k trimming, which predicts how much pruning that domain should tolerate. The contribution is a reproducible reference table for Traditional-Chinese curriculum merging plus a mechanistic reading of why the optimum sits where it does. We expect the Taiwan-studies adapter to be the least redundant and therefore the most damaged by aggressive DARE settings that are harmless on English benchmarks.

Experiments.Description: Identical setup to the primary idea: four TMMLU+ domains (chinese, math, taiwan, science), bf16, device_map={'': 0}, logit-comparison MCQ scoring, four rank-8 LoRA adapters trained with a plain torch loop.
Experiments.Metrics: Base and single-adapter accuracy per domain.

Experiments.Description: Operator sweep at fixed density: task arithmetic, TIES, DARE-TIES, plus simple weight averaging as a floor.
Experiments.Metrics: Mean and per-domain retention for each operator, with three seeds and standard deviations.

Experiments.Description: Density sweep for TIES: trim density in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.0}. Drop-probability sweep for DARE-TIES: p in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9}.
Experiments.Metrics: Retention as a function of density and of p, per domain. Report the argmax density per domain and whether it differs across domains.

Experiments.Description: Redundancy measurement, independent of accuracy. For each domain and each trim density, compute the fraction of the delta's Frobenius norm retained after trimming.
Experiments.Metrics: Norm-retention curve per domain. Test whether the domain ranking by redundancy matches the domain ranking by tolerance to aggressive pruning.

Risk Factors and Limitations: This is a sweep, so its novelty rests on the transfer question rather than on a new method; if the English-derived defaults transfer perfectly, the contribution is a negative result.

The full cross product is large. At the 1B search scale a single merged evaluation is seconds, so the sweep fits the budget, but the 27B confirmation run must be restricted to the argmax settings only.
Three seeds is enough to detect large effects but not small ones; effect sizes below roughly 2 accuracy points should not be interpreted.
